walkthrough: To draw cumulative frequency graphs, always plot the cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary of each interval.

hints: A girl is unable to stand upright in a cave of height 165 cm if her height is strictly greater than 165 cm ($h > 165$).
Read the cumulative frequency for girls at height 165 cm from your graph (approximately 42).
Subtract this value from the total of 60 girls to find how many girls are taller than 165 cm: $60 - 42 = 18$.
Express this count as a percentage of the 60 girls: $\dfrac{18}{60} \times 100\%$.
walkthrough: The cave ceiling is $165\text{ cm}$ high. A student will be unable to stand upright if their height is greater than $165\text{ cm}$.
Step 1: Locate $165\text{ cm}$ on the horizontal axis of your cumulative frequency diagram and move vertically up to meet the girls' curve.
Step 2: Read across to the vertical cumulative frequency axis. The reading is approximately $42$ girls (acceptable range is $41$ to $43$). This means 42 girls are $165\text{ cm}$ or shorter.

Step 3: To find how many girls are taller than $165\text{ cm}$, subtract from the total of 60 girls:
$$\text{Girls taller than } 165\text{ cm} = 60 - 42 = 18$$

Step 4: Convert this count to a percentage:
$$\text{Percentage} = \frac{18}{60} \times 100\% = 30\%$$

hints: Consider the key statistical features prominently displayed on a box plot: median, quartiles, and range.
Think about how easy it is to visually compare the medians and spreads directly without reading values from curves.
State clearly that box-and-whisker plots allow immediate visual comparison of central tendency and spread.
walkthrough: While cumulative frequency graphs display every percentile, parallel box-and-whisker plots summarize the data directly into a five-figure summary.

An advantage of using box-and-whisker plots to compare the groups is that the medians and interquartile ranges are explicitly displayed as lines and boxes. This makes it immediately obvious which group has a higher average height and which group has greater spread, without needing to perform manual lookups on curves.
